newsitem.title: USA: NASD to end mandatory arbitration for bias cases.
newsitem.headline: NASD to end mandatory arbitration for bias cases.

text.p: The National Association of Securities Dealers said Thursday it has decided to stop a Wall Street custom that prevents employees of securities firms from taking their discrimination and harassment claims to court.

The NASD voted on a plan Thursday that must now be approved by the Securities and Exchange Commission, which would eliminate mandatory arbitration for discrimination and harrassment claims made by brokers.

"For cases that allege a violation of a person's civil rights, employees will have the choice to have their claim heard in court," Frank Zarb, chairman, chief exectuvie officer and president of NASD, said in a statement.

Currently, the NASD requires that individuals working for securities firms, as a condition of employment, agree to arbitrate all employment and investor claims rather than take those complaints to court.

Discrimination or sexual harassment claims make up a very small percentage of disputes arbitrated in the securities industry, but the issue has attracted widespread attention in recent months following several high-profile cases.
"Mandatory arbitration effectively guts the civil rights laws," said National Organization for Women President Patricia Ireland, in a statement.

Opponents of the arbitration-only requirement say the practice prevents women, minorities and older workers on Wall Street from enjoying the same protections under U.S. law given to every other U.S. worker.
The new NASD rules, would be effective a year after the SEC approves them, the association said.

In addition to ending the arbitration-only requirement, the NASD said it will continue improving its arbitration system by making sure the panels hearing cases are more diverse and better trained to handle discrimination claims.
The NASD move is a good first step, NOW's Ireland told Reuters, but she maintained that securities firms themselves can still impose an arbitration-only requirement.
"It's a very satifsying benchmark, it's not the end of the campaign," Ireland said. She added that her organization plans to address the issue directly with Wall Street firms.

The Securities Industry Association just last month urged the NASD not to change its arbitration-only requirement, asserting that the practice is cost-effective. Officials there could not be reached for comment on the NASD's latest move.
